problem: Mobile manipulation methods treat navigation and manipulation separately, so they fail when movable obstacles (doors, curtains) must be pushed aside and held open before the base can pass. End-to-end RL for this needs heavy exploration and transfers poorly to real legged robots.
motivation: Obstacles that spring back to their original position require the hand to hold them while the base moves, so the choice of hand pose determines how far the base can advance. Priors from robot kinematics and from visual affordances could cut RL exploration and make sim-to-real transfer feasible.
key_idea: Learn hand positions in image-pixel action space with DDQN, using a precomputed manipulability map as a KL-regularized action prior and a training-free SAM-based affordance mask as an extra state input.
insight: Ablations show the affordance mask is the main driver of both sample efficiency and real-world transfer (real success 0.8 for DDQN-A and DDQN-AP vs 0.1 for DDQN and DDQN-P). The manipulability prior alone does not help in real-world tests, but it does not hurt when combined with affordance, so it acts as a complementary feasibility filter. Failures come mainly from segmentation errors, camera viewpoint shifts during manipulation, and image-to-world projection errors.
method: Manipulability prior: precompute the Spot arm's manipulability w=sqrt(det(JJ^T)) over candidate hand positions, filter IK failures, and project to the camera image with intrinsics/extrinsics to get a pixel-space prior.
KL-regularized DDQN: the loss is the DDQN TD loss plus lambda times a discounted KL between the agent policy and the manipulability prior.
Visual affordance state: Mobile-SAM produces a binary 480x640 mask of manipulable objects online (training-free), fed to the Q-network as s_aff alongside the DINOv2 policy state.
Pixel action space: the action is a pixel (x,y) in the front RGB-D image, projected into a 3D hand target using camera parameters and depth.
Reward: weighted sum of IK-failure penalty, balance penalty, task-specific arm reward, and base translation distance kept with the hand fixed (only once the hand has reached the target).
Tasks: Spot-Reach and Spot-Door in Isaac Sim, plus a real-world Spot-Reach with the same camera model and mounting.

setting.backbone: DDQN Q-network with DINOv2 features and Mobile-SAM affordance masks (frozen foundation models); Q-network trained by RL
setting.training_data: Online RL in Isaac Sim, 4 parallel envs on one RTX 3080; converges in about 4000 steps on Reach; no extra data
setting.action_space: pixel coordinates of the target hand position, projected to a 3D end-effector target; base then moves forward at a given velocity
setting.privileged: none at test time; the manipulability map is precomputed from the robot's known kinematics

numbers.extra: sim-to-real, 10 real-world trials; max base movement distance 0.5 m among successes
numbers.evidence: Table I: Success rate of the methods in real world with 10 trails; DDQN-AP 0.8

numbers_note: Simulation results (Reach, Door) are only shown in training-curve figures. The text says DDQN-AP exceeds 85% success within 1000 steps on Reach. The real-world table gives 0.1 for DDQN and DDQN-P.
results: In simulation, DDQN-AP converges fastest (over 85% success on Reach within ~1000 steps, converging around 4000, versus more than three times as many steps for plain DDQN). In the real world, DDQN-A and DDQN-AP reach 0.8 success against 0.1 for DDQN and DDQN-P, with a max base advance of 0.5 m.
limitations: Relies on segmentation, camera calibration and image-to-world projection; errors in these cause failures.
Camera viewpoint shifts during manipulation (Door task), and the base tends to retreat, giving no positive average movement distance.
Only a simple task with 10 real trials on Reach; the Door task was not tested on the real robot.
